title: LLP versus private limited company: compare control, funding and continuity
excerpt: Compare LLP and private limited company structures around ownership, management, investment and the obligations your business will need to maintain.
content:
An LLP and a private limited company can both support a business with more than one participant, but they organise ownership and decision-making differently. Compare them using the proposed owners, funding plan and governance needs. Neither is automatically the best choice for every small business.

This comparison concerns an Indian LLP and a private company limited by shares. It is a starting point for a discussion with an appropriate company secretary, legal adviser and tax professional, using the actual venture rather than a generic registration package.

Understand the basic ownership distinction

An LLP is a legal entity separate from its partners. Its partnership agreement governs the partners' mutual rights and duties subject to the LLP Act. A company limited by shares uses share ownership and the company-law framework, including its memorandum and articles. LLP Act, MCA explanation of the LLP agreement, Companies Act.

Decision LLP discussion Private company discussion
Ownership Partners, contributions and partnership interests Shareholders, shareholdings and share rights
Management Partners' roles and authority under the agreement and law Directors' authority and shareholder decisions under the governing framework
New participant Admission and terms in the partnership arrangement Proposed share issue or transfer and required approvals
Departure Exit, settlement and continuing rights Share transfer, exit terms and continuing rights
Governance record Agreement, amendments and recorded decisions Articles, ownership records and corporate decisions

The table identifies questions to resolve. It is not a substitute for the legal procedure applying to a particular transaction.

Decide how the founders want to work together

Describe each person's contribution, working role and expected return. Discuss who will approve borrowing, major purchases, new participants and changes to the business. Consider what information each owner needs to review performance.

An LLP agreement should be drafted for the intended relationship. In a company, the constitutional documents and any shareholder arrangements also need to work together. In either structure, an informal understanding can leave important decisions unclear.

For illustration, a technical founder and a funding founder may want different day-to-day roles but shared control over a sale of the business. Explain that intention before documents are prepared. The adviser can then assess how it can be implemented lawfully.

Start the funding comparison with a real plan

Identify whether funding is expected from existing participants, a bank or new investors. If an investor is being considered, ask what ownership instrument, information rights and decision rights it expects. Do not assume every investor accepts the same structure.

Likewise, obtain the lender's requirements for the actual borrower and project. Neither an LLP incorporation certificate nor a private-company certificate guarantees sanction. Financial viability, evidence and the proposed borrowing terms still need review.

Read the business loan document guide to prepare that evidence independently of the entity comparison.

Understand the limits of liability protection

The LLP Act distinguishes an LLP's obligations from a partner's liability solely because of being a partner, while retaining provisions concerning personal wrongful acts and fraud. For a company limited by shares, the Act describes members' liability by reference to unpaid share amounts. LLP liability provisions; company memorandum provisions.

These distinctions do not justify a blanket promise of zero personal risk. Ask the adviser to assess personal guarantees, conduct, role-specific duties and the actual contracts before borrowing or signing commitments.

Compare continuing work and future changes

Request a tailored calendar of accounts, filings, decisions and professional work under each option. Ask how records will be maintained and what the owners must review. Avoid treating an LLP as having no compliance obligations or assuming every company's obligations are identical.

Model tax and distributions using the same assumptions for both structures. Then examine a likely future change, such as an investor joining or a founder leaving. Consider the effect on contracts, assets, approvals and finance before deciding.

title: Reverse charge under GST: review the supply before deciding who pays
excerpt: Use the transaction, supplier, recipient and current notification to assess whether reverse charge under GST needs an accounts review.
content:
Under the reverse charge mechanism, the recipient pays GST for a supply covered by the relevant provisions instead of the usual supplier-payment arrangement. It is a transaction-specific question. The supplier's registration status alone is not enough to decide every case.

Section 9(3) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act provides for notified categories of supply. The current section 9(4) concerns specified classes of registered recipients and specified supplies received from unregistered suppliers. It should not be read as a blanket rule that every purchase from an unregistered person attracts reverse charge. See CBIC's current section 9 text.

Assemble the facts before choosing a tax entry

Start with the actual goods or services supplied. Keep the contract, purchase order, invoice and evidence of the supplier's and recipient's identities. Record registration status, location, transaction value and the relevant dates.

A general ledger label such as “freight”, “legal charges” or “rent” is a starting description, not the entire legal test. The arrangement, parties and applicable notification can matter. Ask the accounts or GST professional to identify the exact basis for the conclusion.

For supplies involving another state or country, the relevant GST framework also needs review. Do not apply an intra-state provision mechanically without considering the nature and location of the supply.

Ask which notification applies

A useful assessment identifies the current notification, entry, conditions and effective date. It explains how the actual supplier and recipient fit those conditions, including any applicable exclusions or choices.

Avoid relying on a table copied from a historical article without checking amendments. The official section 9 text records that subsection (4) was substituted with effect from 1 February 2019. This is one reason an early GST summary can produce the wrong conclusion today. CBIC amendment note.

For illustration, two invoices may both be recorded internally as “professional charges” while relating to different services and recipient circumstances. They need separate classification. Applying the same reverse-charge flag to both without reviewing those facts can create an unsupported tax entry.

Resolve related questions separately

Once applicability is established, ask the responsible professional to determine the valuation, rate, time of supply, payment method, documentation and return treatment. Review input tax credit separately against its own conditions. An expectation that credit may be available does not answer when or how tax must be paid.

Where an invoice appears inconsistent with the assessed treatment, reconcile it with the supplier before relying on it. Keep the explanation and corrected documentation where needed. Do not simply delete supplier-charged tax or create an additional liability without resolving the transaction history.

Make the review repeatable

For recurring transactions, record a short approved treatment note containing:

  • The actual service or goods and the parties involved.
  • The provision and notification considered.
  • The conclusion and its conditions.
  • The documents required to support it.
  • The date and circumstances that should trigger another review.

This makes the next month's check more focused. Revisit the conclusion when the contract, supplier status, recipient status or applicable rules change. A standing accounts rule is useful only while its assumptions remain true.

Connect tax records with project expenditure

If the purchase also appears in a loan or subsidy file, reconcile its accounting treatment with the cost schedule used there. Tax paid, recoverable credit and eligible expenditure are different questions. A GST conclusion does not automatically establish the amount accepted by a lender or subsidy scheme.

Read the loan document guide and subsidy application mistakes for the wider evidence file. Specific GST advice and filings should remain with the professional responsible for tax compliance.

title: Textile interest subsidy in Haryana: prepare the annual loan evidence
excerpt: Understand how to organise the loan, repayment and project records needed to assess a Haryana textile interest subsidy claim.
content:
A textile interest subsidy claim needs evidence about the eligible project and the interest paid on the relevant loan. A loan sanction letter alone cannot establish the annual claim amount. Keep the borrowing, repayment record and project investment connected throughout the claim period.

Haryana's July 2023 interest subsidy notification sets out different provisions for textile MSMEs and textile machine manufacturers. The categories should not be mixed. Its bank certificate format asks for loan, disbursement, repayment and interest information, including the exclusion of penal interest from the certified claim calculation. Read the interest subsidy notification.

The policy and its notified schemes were extended through 18 December 2026 by a May 2025 notification. The extension should be read with the scheme conditions and the dates relevant to the individual project. See the extension notification.

Confirm the project category before calculating interest

Describe the manufacturing activity, MSME position, exact location and whether the investment is a new unit or qualifying expansion. Record the date production started and identify the investment financed by the loan.

The Textile Interest Subsidy scheme page explains the scheme route. Do not borrow a percentage, annual cap or benefit period from another textile category. A unit making textile machinery requires a different category check from a unit using that machinery to manufacture textiles.

For an expansion, explain what existed before the project and what changed. The factory's total borrowing is not necessarily the same as the borrowing relevant to the assessed expansion.

Build a loan record that can be reconciled

Keep a separate record for each loan proposed for review. Include the sanction letter, amendments, disbursement schedule, account statements and lender details. Describe the purpose of the loan and the assets or work it financed.

Ask the bank for the certificate required by the applicable claim format. Give it the relevant financial year and loan reference. A general interest certificate supplied for accounting purposes may not answer every question in the scheme's prescribed format.

Check the certificate against your accounts. Resolve differences in the borrower name, account number, loan amount, disbursement dates and interest figures before filing. Keep an explanation for corrections instead of silently replacing one version of the record.

Distinguish interest from other bank debits

A loan account can contain principal repayments, ordinary interest, penal charges, processing fees and other debits. These are not one interchangeable expense.

For illustration, a statement showing a total debit of ₹12 lakh does not mean ₹12 lakh is interest eligible for assistance. Part may be principal and part may be charges. The claim needs a supported breakdown and the calculation permitted by the scheme, rather than a percentage applied to the whole debit.

If the loan was restructured, refinanced, transferred or irregular during the year, disclose that history. Ask how the actual facts affect the claim. Do not assume a fresh bank certificate removes a scheme condition or a repayment issue.

Maintain the project evidence as well as the bank evidence

Keep the relevant enterprise records, approvals, investment schedule and production evidence with the annual claim papers. Record changes in ownership, location, capacity or project assets. A correct interest total cannot repair an unresolved question about the applicant or project.

Set a calendar from the current claim provisions and retain proof of submission. If a deadline may have passed, check any permitted route using the actual facts. Do not assume every delay is condonable.

Textile capital investment subsidy is a separate claim route. Maintain distinct calculations and check the interaction of assistance instead of merging capital expenditure and interest into one unsupported total.

Make the review easy to follow

Prepare a one-page summary showing the project, loan, financial year, interest figure, supporting bank certificate and unresolved questions. Seven subsidy application mistakes can help you check the wider file.
